d.title: is versus ==, stepped
d.caption: == asks whether two objects have equal value; is asks whether they are the same object. Two equal lists are not identical; small integers and interned strings sometimes are, which is why is 'appears to work' until it does not.

d.title: and / or return an operand, not a bool
d.caption: or returns the first truthy operand (or the last one); and returns the first falsy operand (or the last one). That is why name or 'anon' works as a default, and why it fails when the empty string is a valid value.

d.title: The mutable default, stepped
d.caption: The default list is created once when def runs and shared by every call that omits the argument. The fix — None as the default and a fresh list inside — gives each call its own.

steps.code: def g(x, items=None): items = items or []

d.title: The loop else, stepped
d.caption: Searching for 7 in [3, 5, 9]: the loop runs to exhaustion, so else runs and reports 'not found'. Searching for 5, break fires on the second pass and else is skipped.

steps.code: for x in [3, 5, 9]: if x == 7: break
for x in [3, 5, 9]: if x == 5: break

d.title: When a comprehension stops helping
d.caption: A comprehension is for building one collection from one iterable with at most one condition. Side effects, nested logic and three-level nesting belong in a loop, where a reader can breathe.

columns.title: keep the comprehension
items: [f(x) for x in xs if ok(x)]
fits on a line or two

d.title: UnboundLocalError: assignment decides at compile time
d.caption: Because count is assigned somewhere in f, the compiler makes it local for the whole function; the read on the first line then finds an unassigned local. global (or nonlocal for an enclosing scope) changes the decision.

steps.code: def g(): global count; count += 1; g()

d.title: A closure with state, stepped
d.caption: nonlocal lets inner rebind count in the enclosing cell. Each call to make_counter creates a new cell, so c1 and c2 count independently.

d.title: fact(4), unwound
d.caption: Each call waits for the one below it; the base case returns 1 and the results multiply back up through the frames. The stack is deepest — four frames — just before the first return.

d.title: Instance attribute shadows class attribute
d.caption: Reading finds the class attribute through the instance; assigning through the instance creates an instance attribute that shadows it for that instance only. The mutable class attribute, appended to, is shared by all.

d.title: Cooperative __init__ through the MRO
d.caption: Each __init__ calls super().__init__(**kwargs) and takes only its own arguments; super() follows the MRO, not the parent, so every class in the diamond runs exactly once.

items.label: D.__init__(name, size, colour)
items.desc: takes name, passes the rest up

items.label: super() → C.__init__(colour)
items.desc: takes colour — next in the MRO, not B's parent

items.label: object.__init__()
items.desc: accepts no arguments: **kwargs must be empty by here

d.title: __repr__ versus __str__
d.caption: repr is for the developer and should be unambiguous, ideally valid Python; str is for the user. Define __repr__ first — str falls back to it, containers use it, and debuggers show it.

columns.title: __repr__
items: shown in the REPL, lists, tracebacks

d.title: The walrus operator in a loop
d.caption: := binds a name inside an expression, so the read-then-test pattern needs no separate assignment line. The name is visible after the loop as well.

d.title: A generator runs only when asked
d.caption: Calling gen() executes nothing; each next() runs the body to the next yield and pauses there with its locals intact. After the last yield, the next call raises StopIteration.

d.title: Which clauses run
d.caption: Four ways a try block can end, and which of except, else and finally run in each. finally runs even when the block returns or raises something uncaught.

steps.code: try body raises a matching exception
try body raises an unmatched exception

d.title: Two timeouts, two meanings
d.caption: The connect timeout bounds how long to wait for the TCP handshake; the read timeout bounds the wait for each chunk of the response. A single number sets both; a slow upstream needs them chosen separately.

columns.title: connect timeout
items: waiting for the socket to open
fails fast on a dead host

columns.title: read timeout
items: matches the upstream's slowest honest response

columns.title: total deadline
items: what the caller actually cares about
enforce with asyncio.timeout or a wall-clock check

d.title: sys.path depends on how you ran it
d.caption: python pkg/mod.py puts pkg/ first on sys.path and the package's own imports break; python -m pkg.mod puts the current directory first and everything resolves. The file is the same; the search path is not.

steps.note: pkg is not on the path

d.title: A three-stage pipeline pulls one item at a time
d.caption: The consumer's next() pulls from the last stage, which pulls from the one before it, back to the source. One item is in flight; memory stays flat however large the file.

d.title: Narrowing: the checker tracks what it knows
d.caption: After isinstance, an early return or a None check, the type checker refines the declared type inside that branch. Narrowing is why Optional[str] can be used safely without a cast.

steps.code: def g(v: int | str): if isinstance(v, int): v + 1

d.title: The simpler hooks before a metaclass
d.caption: Most 'I need a metaclass' problems are solved by a hook that already exists. __init_subclass__ sees every subclass as it is created; __set_name__ tells a descriptor its attribute name; a class decorator rewrites a class after the fact.

d.title: A weak reference does not keep its target alive
d.caption: cache holds a weakref to the object; when the last strong reference (obj) is dropped the object is freed and the weakref returns None. Caches and observer lists use this to avoid pinning objects in memory.

d.title: Fixture scopes across a test session
d.caption: A session-scoped fixture is built once and torn down at the end; a module-scoped one per test file; a function-scoped one per test. Wider scope is faster and shares state — choose the narrowest that is not too slow.

d.title: The test-double taxonomy
d.caption: Names that are used interchangeably and should not be. A mock asserts on how it was called; a stub just answers; a fake works for real, in miniature.

d.title: tottime versus cumtime
d.caption: tottime is time inside the function itself; cumtime includes everything it called. Sort by tottime to find the function doing the work; by cumtime to find the caller responsible for it.

columns.title: tottime
items: sort here to find the hot function

columns.title: cumtime
items: sort here to find the hot path
a hot root: call it less

d.title: Invalidation, or a cache is a bug with a delay
d.caption: Every cached value is a claim that the underlying data has not changed. Something has to make that true: an explicit clear on write, a TTL, or a key that changes with the data.

items.label: invalidate on write
items.desc: f.cache_clear() or delete the key when the source changes

items.label: time to live
items.desc: accept staleness for a bounded time — TTLCache, Redis EX

items.label: versioned key
items.desc: put the data's version or hash in the key; old entries age out

items.label: never cache what changes under you
items.desc: lru_cache on a method reading self.state is a classic trap

d.title: Start methods
d.caption: fork copies the parent's memory instantly but inherits its locks and threads — unsafe with threads; spawn starts a fresh interpreter and pickles everything, which is slower but safe. macOS and Windows default to spawn; Linux switched its default in 3.14.

columns.title: fork
items: inherits locks, open files, threads — deadlock risk

columns.title: spawn
items: imports the module again — guard with __main__

columns.title: forkserver
items: a clean server process forks on request

d.title: Cancellation is cooperative
d.caption: task.cancel() schedules a CancelledError to be raised at the task's next await. The task can clean up in finally, but it must not swallow the error, or the caller waits forever.

items.label: task.cancel()
items.desc: marks the task; nothing happens yet

items.label: finally: blocks run
items.desc: close connections, release locks — keep it short

items.label: the error propagates
items.desc: except CancelledError: pass is the bug — re-raise

d.title: Cursor pagination
d.caption: Each page carries an opaque cursor for the next one; the client follows it until there is none. No page numbers to drift when rows are inserted, and each request is O(1) for the server.

d.title: The four mistakes
d.caption: Each one passes a demo and fails in production. The signature is the contract; response_model is what makes the contract true on the way out.

d.title: async def or def, by what the handler does
d.caption: FastAPI runs a plain def handler in a thread pool and an async def on the event loop. The wrong choice is silent: an async def that calls a synchronous library stalls every request.

cells.text: blocks a thread — use a process or queue

d.title: Row by row versus a batch
d.caption: A thousand single-row INSERTs are a thousand round trips; executemany or a multi-row VALUES sends them in one. COPY is faster still for bulk loads.

d.title: A composite index is used left to right
d.caption: An index on (customer_id, created_at) serves WHERE customer_id = ? and WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ?, but not WHERE created_at > ? alone — the leading column must be constrained.
d.label: INDEX (customer_id, created_at, status): a query on created_at alone cannot use it

d.title: The four golden signals
d.caption: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation. If a dashboard shows these four per service, most incidents are visible before the pager goes off.

columns.title: latency
items: of successful and failed requests separately

d.title: WSGI and ASGI: the server, the interface, the app
d.caption: A web server speaks HTTP to the world and calls your application through an interface. WSGI is synchronous — one call, one response; ASGI is asynchronous and also carries WebSockets and lifespan events.

d.title: Views share memory; copies do not
d.caption: A slice of a NumPy array is a view onto the same buffer: writing through it changes the original. Fancy indexing and .copy() allocate a new buffer.

d.title: A ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline
d.caption: Numeric columns are imputed and scaled, categorical columns one-hot encoded, the two blocks concatenated, and the model fit on the result — one object that fits and predicts consistently.

d.title: The context window is a budget
d.caption: System prompt, retrieved context, the conversation so far and the answer all share one window. Count tokens before the call and leave room for the response, or the model truncates from the wrong end.
d.label: 8,000-token window: what is reserved for the answer is what the model can say

d.title: Detecting a cycle in a directed graph
d.caption: DFS colours nodes white (unvisited), grey (on the current path) and black (finished). Reaching a grey node from the current path is a back edge — a cycle. Topological sort is the same walk with the finish order reversed.
